source.title: OmniLearn: A Framework for Distributed Deep Learning Over Heterogeneous Clusters

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares held-out accuracy under uniform and variable per-worker batch sizes in heterogeneous distributed training. This is a conceptual test of batch-size adaptation, though it does not measure the training-to-test gap or isolate large-batch effects at a fixed epoch budget.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for uniform batching and variable batching. Rows below cover ASP test-accuracy comparisons at HL4 and HL8. The paper also reports batch-scaling effects on BSP accuracy, but does not provide a matching uniform-batching result for those same heterogeneous settings in the cited tables. Results it cites about large-batch generalization are not recorded as this study's findings.
record.test_reason: OmniLearn uses prior large-batch generalization findings to constrain batch sizes, then evaluates its distributed-training method. It does not compare large versus small batches under a fixed epoch budget or establish a large-batch penalty that its adaptations remove. BSP preserves the global batch size; ASP comparisons change worker batch allocation, learning rates and gradient staleness together.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that variable and dynamic batching improve training performance on heterogeneous clusters. Variable batching improves ASP accuracy across the matched heterogeneous configurations, while slightly degrading BSP accuracy despite improving parallel efficiency. Weighted gradient aggregation and learning-rate scaling yield gains of up to 10.21 and 6.9 percentage points, respectively; the conclusion reports average training speedup of 26% with comparable convergence targets.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts per-worker batch sizes to resource heterogeneity and compares distributed-training performance; it does not use the original claim's memorization or generalization-gap measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported ASP accuracy changes with model and heterogeneity level. The paper notes that accuracy can suffer at HL8 for ResNet50 and VGG11 relative to HL1 or HL4, attributing this to remaining staleness.

fits_no_version.finding: ASP variable batching with learning-rate scaling improves reported test accuracy over uniform batching in all eight matched heterogeneous configurations. Gains range from 3.94 to 15.72 percentage points, and the authors attribute improvements primarily to reduced staleness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Allocating worker batch sizes according to compute resources, together with batch-dependent learning rates, can improve asynchronous distributed-training accuracy on heterogeneous clusters.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems
record.problems: The matched batch-size comparisons are in heterogeneous ASP settings and do not isolate batch size from the distributed-training and staleness conditions. The paper reports test accuracy but not training error or the training-to-test gap; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No matched ASP HL1 rows were retained because they are the reference condition rather than the heterogeneous settings relevant to the comparison. Other results in Tables III, V and VI concern BSP variable-batching or additional gradient and learning-rate scaling comparisons, rather than the matched ASP uniform-versus-variable comparison extracted here.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed to fit training data.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Large-versus-small-batch held-out performance at fixed epoch budgets, workload-dependent batch thresholds, and whether recipe adaptations remove an established large-batch penalty.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness correlations with generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Accuracy after removing memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: All eight extracted accuracy pairs match Tables II and IV. Their state becomes cannot_determine because they cannot establish a claim-version effect, despite showing clear method improvements. Section IV-A specifies momentum, weight decay and learning-rate schedules for every model; initialization from scratch is not explicitly established. Contrary to the record's gate note, Section III-A explicitly identifies HL1 in Table III as the uniform-batching BSP accuracy baseline across heterogeneity levels. Those comparisons still preserve global batch size and do not test V5. A training-to-test gap measurement is not required for V5; the decisive omissions are the relevant batch-size contrast and fixed epoch budget.

versions.untested_parts: Large-batch training versus small-batch training at a fixed epoch budget; training error and the training-to-test gap.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
